title: Rasa, Reflexivity, Research and Reciprocal Anthropology
content: Anthropology knows by coming close, yet its main instrument for examining that closeness, reflexivity, keeps the researcher at a remove. Reflexivity asks the ethnographer to scrutinise the self and leaves open what the ethnographer owes. This article brings rasa, the classical Indian account of knowing as tasting, into that debate. Rasa has long been studied in anthropology as emotion, devotion and performance, but almost always as an object of study and seldom as a way of understanding the researcher’s own relation to the field. Framed by Indigenous Gnoseology, which holds that knowing is wider than epistemology, and in dialogue with Kasulis’s distinction between integrity and intimacy, we read reflexivity as a practice that stays within epistemology and rasa as an articulation of intimate knowing. We analyse a purposively assembled corpus of 50 works on rasa and cognate concepts published since the 1950s, coding each for where rasa sits, the mode of knowing it describes, and whether obligation to the people studied is addressed. Rasa is the object of study in 32 of the 50 works and grounds the researcher’s own knowing in only 12; practitioner-scholars who learned by tasting report that learning as background; and the knowing the corpus describes is gnoseological yet named epistemology. Obligation to the people studied is mentioned in four works, none of which treats rasa as an object, and is developed in none. We argue that intimacy without obligation can still extract. Drawing on long-term fieldwork with Rakhain and Rohingya communities, we propose reciprocal anthropology, practised as asking before tasting, returning what was tasted, and keeping the relation after exit, as the step that completes what reflexivity and intimacy leave open.
